Q: Why should I use core.autocrlf=true in Git? A:

Modern Solution (2026): Use .gitattributes instead of core.autocrlf

Relying on core.autocrlf (true or false) is error-prone because it requires every developer on a team to configure their local Git settings correctly.

The modern standard is to use a .gitattributes file at the root of your repository. This file is tracked in Git and enforces line-ending rules automatically for everyone on Windows, macOS, and Linux.

Example .gitattributes:

# Default rule: Auto-detect text files and normalize line endings to LF
* text=auto eol=lf

# Windows batch files require CRLF
*.bat text eol=crlf
*.cmd text eol=crlf

# Shell scripts require LF
*.sh text eol=lf

After adding this file, normalize your repository once:

git add --renormalize .
git commit -m "style: enforce line endings with .gitattributes"

Why this is better:

  1. No need to ask developers to set core.autocrlf.
  2. Works consistently across all operating systems.
  3. Prevents line-ending churn in git commits.

Q: Android 16 Photo Picker: Image remains pre-selected in "Limited Access" after app reinstall, but the app cannot access it A:

This is expected Android 16 behavior: after reinstall, the old app’s URI grants are no longer valid, even if Photo Picker shows the images pre-selected.
Treat the pre-selection as UI state, not as proof that your new installation can access those URIs.
Request the appropriate media permission again or let the user reselect the photos; don’t rely on persisted URI grants surviving an uninstall/reinstall.
For long-term URI access, use the documented persistence mechanism where supported, but handle cases where the grant is unavailable.

Q: Mockito when and verify method difference A:

1) When you are using mocks, you are creating a simulation of the class in place of the actual class. Since the object so created doesn't understand what to do when a certain method of the class is called, you need to use when/then to simulate the behavior. The answer to this is NO since you are specifying the behavior that needs to be executed in your test case. Real behavior will be executed when you make an object of the class using the new constructor or when you use @Spy to replicate actual behavior wherever possible.

2) When you specify the below line in your test case, you are instructing the runner to return 50 whenever add() is called with the arguments 10, 20. 

when(mockedObject.add(10,20)).thenReturn(50);

So yes if you write an assert as mentioned below your test will pass since you mentioned that you need the method to return 50 and not the default value:

assertEquals(50, mockedObject.add(10,20));

3) You cannot write when thenReturn for void methods. Mockito will throw error saying 'The method when(T) in the type Mockito is not applicable for the arguments (void)'. For void methods, max you can do is verify if a method has been called or not. I believe you are testing a method that does return something and is not void. Please do not confuse return type of test case with return types of methods inside them.

You can also use doNothing() or doAnswer() with void methods in case you need to override something specific in those.

4) It checks that the methods is called on mocked object or not with same parameter and check the call to the method as only 1 times, right? - Right

verify as I mentioned in 3) is mostly used for testing void methods and is a value add in other tests where assertions would be enough most of the times. You cannot write an assert when the method returns nothing. That's where verify comes into picture.

Q: How to run wsgi along the side of the daphne ASGI for django channels? A:

Q1.

How can I get Django WSGI request instead of ASGI request in my normal function view request (like def index(request):)? Or if we install Django channels, every request becomes an ASGI request?

No, if you install Django Channels, every request doesn't automatically become ASGI. But if you install Daphne at the top of your settings.INSTALLED_APPS, Daphne will then replace the usual runserver command with its own command which spins up an ASGI server.[Django Channels] So if you want to keep using Django's runserver command, do not install Daphne at the top of your settings.INSTALLED_APPS.

This means that your method of spinning up an ASGI server will now default to: daphne myproject.asgi:application invoked from the root directory of your project (same directory as manage.py).

Q2.

What is the use of the python manage.py runworker command?

Keep in mind that it is not a built-in Django management command but is provided by Django Channels when installed in a project.

It runs background workers that process tasks off the Django Channels layer. This means that it can handle messages sent to specific channel types (e.g., WebSockets, background jobs). And it is commonly used in real-time applications like chat apps, live notifications, and task processing.

Q: Web Scraping using Python Beautiful Soup - how to scrape data from multiple pages if URL does not change for each page? A:

. That reviewlist.html?...&offset=10 endpoint is the AJAX call Booking uses for its reviews, and the offset is the pagination. So you can drop Selenium here and just loop that endpoint with requests, bumping the offset until a page comes back empty. (I ended up wrapping that same endpoint in StayingAPI because Booking's review markup kept moving, so I'm biased, but for a one-off the loop below is all you need.)

import requests

from bs4 import BeautifulSoup

base = "https://www.booking.com/reviewlist.html"

params = {

"aid"`: "304142", "pagename": "great-world-service-apartments",`

"type"`: "total", "rows": 10, "cc1": "sg", "offset": 0,`

\# copy label/sid/etc. from your working URL

}

headers = {"User-Agent": "Mozilla/5.0 (Windows NT 10.0; Win64; x64)"}

reviews = []

with requests.Session() as s:

while` True:`

    r `= s.get(base, params=params, headers=headers)`

    blocks `= BeautifulSoup(r.text, "html.parser").select(".review_list_new_item_block")`

    if` not blocks:`

        break

    reviews`.extend(b.get_text(" ", strip=True) for b in blocks)`

    params`["offset"] += params["rows"]`

print(len(reviews))

Confirm the review-block selector against your own response, since Booking's classes shift. And looping the offset until you hit an empty page beats reading that page-number list you found, because it stops itself on the last page, so you don't need to know the count up front.

Q: Best way to iterate in a triangular fashion over a self-crossproduct of a container A:

First upgrade: from C++11 on, you can use range based for(foreach) for cleaner syntax, and bounds safety:

for(auto& d1 : my_data)
    for(auto& d2: my_data)
       use(d1, d2);

The iterators are basically programmer invisible, reducing probability of common pitfalls.

Combining C++20 <ranges> with structured binding from C++17 allows for simpler expresion of Cartesian product:

#include <ranges>
for( auto [d1, d2, d3] 
   : std::views::cartesian_product
   ( my_data1, my_data1, my_data2 ) )
   use(d1, d2, d3);

It's possible to use views as multi-references to original containers too:

auto cart_prod 
= std::views::cartesian_product
  ( my_data, my_data );

for(auto [d1, d2]: cart_prod)
    use(d1, d2);

The specific case of C++23 cartesian_product is unfortunately suboptimal in terms of performance. Compared to that, the rest of <ranges> is a great tool for clean and efficient development. However The performance deficiency of cartesian_product seems to have slowed down adoption of other triangular views that you mentioned. It's possible to define limited versions of these views in own library using C++23 std::ranges::view_interface and std::ranges::range_adaptor_closure.

Edit #1:

For now, the simplest possible form of upper triangular iteration is nested for:

auto b_data
= orig_b_data
| std::views::all;

auto ib = b_data.begin();
for( auto& a : a_data )
    for( auto& b
       : std::views::subrange
         (ib++, b_data.end())
       ) uptriangle(a,b);

To drop diagonal, just change the initialization:

auto b_data
= orig_b_data
| std::views::drop(1);

In order to make bottom triangle change the subrange bounds:

std::views::subrange
( b_data.begin(), ib++ )

Now if the initialization takes all, the digonal is dropped in the bottom triangle; otherwise if the drop(1) is used, the diagonal is included. In short words, changing the subrange bounds as above complements the iteration on top triangle.

Edit #2: In order to avoid UB ar the end of increment oparation, you can use std::ranged::next:

{ std::views::subrange
  ( ib, b_data.end() );
  ib =std::ranged::next
  (ib, b_data.end() ); };

This might look too verbose but the end iterator is always a pain the neck. I hope the implementation of cartesian_product gets optimized, so the triangular views get a chance for standardization, simplifying the composition.
